sceneHappening: One sacrifice for all time; a call to draw near, to hold on, and to endure, with a solemn warning against willful sin
summary: "For the law, having a shadow of the good to come, not the very image of the things, can never with the same sacrifices year by year, which they offer continually, make perfect those who draw near... But in those sacrifices there is a yearly reminder of sins. For it is impossible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sins." So Christ, coming into the world, says (quoting Psalm 40): "You didn't desire sacrifice and offering, but you prepared a body for me... Behold, I have come... to do your will, O God." "By which will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all." "Every priest indeed stands day by day serving and often offering the same sacrifices which can never take away sins, but he, when he had offered one sacrifice for sins forever, sat down on the right hand of God... For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are being sanctified." The new covenant promise follows again: "I will remember their sins and their iniquities no more... Now where remission of these is, there is no more offering for sin." Then comes the call: "Having therefore, brothers, boldness to enter into the holy place by the blood of Jesus, by the way which he dedicated for us, a new and living way, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh, and having a great priest over God's house, let's draw near with a true heart in fullness of faith... let's hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering; for he who promised is faithful. Let's consider how to provoke one another to love and good works, not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is, but exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching." Then the warning: "For if we sin willfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remains no more a sacrifice for sins, but a certain fearful expectation of judgment... It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God." The readers are to remember "the former days" of suffering and joyful loss, and not to "throw away your boldness, which has a great reward. For you need endurance... 'In a very little while, he who comes will come, and will not wait. But the righteous will live by faith. If he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.' But we are not of those who shrink back to destruction, but of those who have faith to the saving of the soul."
whySettingMatters: This chapter brings the long argument about priesthood and sacrifice to a close and turns it into a call. The quotation from Psalm 40:6-8 follows the Greek version, which reads "you prepared a body for me," where the Hebrew has "you have opened my ears"; the writer reads it as Christ's own words at the incarnation. The statement that Christ "sat down" (10:12) contrasts with the standing priests: his work is finished. "Perfected forever those who are being sanctified" (10:14) holds together a completed act and an ongoing process. The three exhortations in 10:22-24, beginning "let's draw near... hold fast... consider," are among the central statements of the letter's faith, hope, and love. "Not forsaking our own assembling together" (10:25) shows that some in the community were staying away, perhaps from fear of being identified; the "Day" is the day of the Lord (compare 9:28). The second solemn warning, 10:26-31, is related to 6:4-8 and is debated in the same way. "Sin willfully" echoes the Old Testament category of sins done "with a high hand" (Numbers 15:30-31), for which no sacrifice was provided. The picture of fire and "fearful expectation of judgment" is set beside a reminder of the readers' own earlier steadfastness (10:32-34): they once accepted the seizure of their property with joy, so they know how to endure. The quotation in 10:37-38 combines Isaiah 26:20 with Habakkuk 2:3-4, the verse Paul also uses in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11.

people.note: Came to do God's will, offered one sacrifice, and sat down.
Calls the readers to draw near, hold fast, and endure.
Reminded of earlier suffering and urged not to shrink back.
His law is cited: whoever disregards it dies on two or three witnesses.

questions: The old sacrifices were "a yearly reminder of sins." What does it mean that Christ's one sacrifice allows sins to be remembered no more?
"Let's consider how to provoke one another to love and good works." What would it look like to provoke each other in that way?
"Not forsaking our own assembling together." What pressures keep people away from the gathering, and how does the passage answer them?
The readers once "joyfully accepted the plundering of your possessions." What can a community draw on from its own past endurance?
